item.title: Why Bilingual Brains Switch Languages Without Asking
item.description:
Cognition

Why Bilingual Brains Switch Languages Without Asking

New brain research explains why two languages sometimes collide mid-sentence.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Bilingual brains manage two active language systems at every moment.
  • Switching languages uses the same brain regions as any executive task.
  • A new 2026 study found one shared grammar system, not separate ones.
  • Mixing languages mid-sentence is a sign of control, not confusion.
A silent workout: Behind every casual conversation, a bilingual brain is constantly activating and suppressing language systems in milliseconds.
Source: Mimi Thian / Unsplash

You're mid-sentence in one language when a word from another shows up instead. Or you reach for a word in your first language and find it in your second one first. Or you notice you feel like a slightly different version of yourself depending on which language you're speaking.

None of that means you're confused, and it doesn't mean either language is slipping. I switch between Spanish and English so often that I sometimes finish a sentence without knowing which one I started it in. It's your brain doing exactly what it was built to do: run two active language systems at once, and occasionally cross the border between them without asking permission first.

Why Language-Switching Sometimes Happens Mid-Sentence

Code-switching, moving between languages mid-conversation, mid-sentence, sometimes mid-word, gets misread constantly as a lapse, or as a failure to fully master either language.

The research says the opposite. A 2022 meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies found that switching languages activates the same brain regions the brain uses for any high-level executive task: conflict monitoring, inhibition, cognitive control (Jiao et al., 2022). Switching languages isn't a glitch. It's an executive function task, the same kind of mental gear-change involved in any competing demand, and like any executive task, it has a cost.

The prefrontal cortex has to actively suppress the language you're not using while keeping the one you are using active. When both languages are highly activated and that suppression isn't complete, mixing happens. Not because one language is bleeding through by accident, but because both systems are running at once, and the brain takes whichever route is fastest, even when that route crosses a language border.

What Brand New Research Just Added

A study published this June adds a layer that wasn't there before (Chen & Blanco-Elorrieta, 2026). Using MEG scans, which track brain activity down to the millisecond, researchers watched fluent Spanish-English bilinguals apply grammar rules, like turning a singular word into a plural, in both languages.

The same left-side brain network handled the grammatical shift every time, regardless of which language was being spoken. The pattern held even when participants were given entirely invented words their brains had never encountered before.

That's a striking piece of evidence: Bilinguals don't appear to run two separate grammar systems side by side; instead, they seem to run one abstract, reusable grammatical operation that gets applied to whichever language happens to be active. Less like having two engines under the hood, more like one engine that can read two different maps.

What This Means If You Live This Every Day

If you've ever felt embarrassed reaching for a word in the "wrong" language, or worried that mixing means you're losing fluency in one of your languages, this research points the other way entirely.

The mixing isn't a sign your languages are deteriorating into each other. It's a sign of a brain efficiently running two active systems through shared machinery, taking the fastest available route, and sometimes that route happens to run straight through the middle of a sentence.

item.title: Summer + Co-parenting = Can Cause Anxiety
item.description:
Divorce

Summer + Co-parenting = Can Cause Anxiety

Summer's freedom for children can create unexpected stress for co-parents.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Summer often brings uncertainty and logistical challenges that can increase co-parenting stress.
  • Planning ahead can reduce conflict and create a more predictable experience for children.
  • Focusing on your child's experience, not parental competition, can make summer more enjoyable for all.

For children, summer often means freedom: no homework, no early alarms, and more time to relax, travel, and spend time with family and friends. For co-parents, however, summer can bring an entirely different set of emotions.

The school year provides structure. Summer removes much of that structure and replaces it with camps, vacations, family gatherings, changing work schedules, and a host of decisions that require coordination between households. Even co-parents who communicate well during the school year may find themselves feeling stressed as summer approaches.

Questions often arise quickly: Who is paying for camp? Can a planned vacation be changed because of a family event? What happens if a child gets sick before travel? How much information should be shared about travel plans?

These issues are not just logistical. They can trigger anxiety, particularly for parents who already struggle with communication, trust, or conflict after divorce.

Why Summer Feels Different

Many parents experience increased anxiety when routines change. During the school year, there are established schedules, predictable exchanges, and fewer opportunities for scheduling disputes. Summer often requires greater flexibility and more communication.

In some families, parents worry about losing time with their children. Others worry about whether plans will be respected or whether disagreements will disrupt the child's summer experience. When emotions run high, even minor scheduling issues can feel much larger than they really are.

The good news is that preparation can significantly reduce stress.

Start the Conversation Early

One of the most effective ways to reduce summer conflict is to begin planning well in advance. Early conversations give both parents an opportunity to discuss vacation plans, camps, special events, and scheduling preferences before commitments are made.

When parents communicate early, they are more likely to feel heard and less likely to perceive scheduling requests as demands or last-minute surprises.

Review Existing Agreements

If a custody agreement or parenting plan exists, it is likely a court order and must be followed unless the agreement or plan allows for change and flexibility. Many parenting agreements contain provisions regarding vacation schedules, notice requirements, and holiday allocations.

Understanding the existing framework can help prevent unnecessary disagreements and create realistic expectations for both parents.

Create a Detailed Summer Schedule

Children tend to thrive when they know what to expect. A clear schedule benefits everyone involved.

Consider including:

  • Vacation periods for each parent
  • Camps and extracurricular activities
  • Family celebrations and reunions
  • Summer holidays
  • Transportation arrangements
  • Exchange dates, times, and locations

The more clarity there is at the beginning of the summer, the fewer opportunities there are for confusion later.

Be Transparent About Travel

Travel is often one of the most exciting parts of summer—and one of the most common sources of co-parenting conflict.

Providing a detailed itinerary can help reduce anxiety and build trust. Parents should consider sharing flight information, lodging details, emergency contact information, and general travel plans well before departure.

Transparency is not simply about complying with an agreement. It can reassure both parents and allow everyone to focus on what matters most: ensuring that children enjoy meaningful experiences with each side of the family.

Have a Backup Plan

Even the most carefully organized summer can be disrupted by illness, weather, travel delays, or unexpected work obligations.

Discussing contingency plans in advance can prevent a temporary problem from becoming a larger conflict. When parents agree ahead of time on how unexpected situations will be handled, they are often better able to respond calmly when challenges arise.

Keep the Focus on the Child

Summer scheduling can sometimes become a source of competition between parents. It is easy to become focused on who has more time, who planned first, or whose vacation is more exciting.

Children, however, generally benefit most when they are free to enjoy time with both parents without feeling caught in the middle.

When co-parents approach summer planning with flexibility, respect, and a shared commitment to their child's well-being, children are more likely to experience summer as it is meant to be experienced: a season of connection, growth, and enjoyment.

And as I often say: Please don't forget to take care of yourself during this stressful period! Managing schedules, expectations, and emotions can be exhausting. A little preparation and self-compassion can go a long way.

This post is for educational purposes only and should not be construed as legal advice. Every family situation is unique. If you have questions about your custody arrangement, consult a qualified family law attorney in your area.

item.title: When Therapists Get It Wrong
item.description:
Therapy

When Therapists Get It Wrong

Openness and feedback are vital for meaningful therapy outcomes.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Therapists are human and make mistakes, and some behaviours are unacceptable.
  • Others may go unnoticed by the therapist.
  • Clients can take the opportunity to say what might be going wrong.
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

I routinely offer a brief phone chat with prospective clients—I explain our approach, hear about the concern that has led them to consider therapy, and build positive expectations about potential outcomes. But I had never received such a grilling as I did from Afra.

It turned out that she had been badly let down by a previous therapist, who had quite suddenly blanked her—not returning her emails and calls to make a next appointment. She could see online that the therapist was still practising, and the therapist had given no indication, Afra claimed, that she didn’t think it a good idea to continue working with Afra.

This seemed quite shocking to me, a behaviour which surely went against the code of ethics of whatever regulatory body that therapist was governed by. Any possibility that Afra might have been unusually demanding or difficult to work with was quickly dispelled by our own sessions together.

I have also had new clients tell me of previous therapy where the therapist sometimes talked about their own problems instead of those of the client.

No therapist is perfect. Fifteen years ago, I read research on embarrassing and unprofessional behaviours a therapist might display during a session, after which some of the therapists felt so terrible that they carried on as if nothing had happened.1 The researchers surveyed 93 experienced, practising psychotherapists (who used therapeutic methods ranging from psychodynamic-analytical to cognitive-behavioural, interpersonal and integrative).

The therapists owned up to slips such as using inappropriate language; consistently calling the client by the wrong name until the client pointed it out; and missing the chair when going to sit down. However, most common were double-booking; confusing one client’s personal information with another’s; introducing a new therapeutic intervention that had been introduced the previous week (and a supplied handout); appearing visibly tired and unfocused; and arriving late.

Also relatively common—amazingly, to me—was falling asleep during the session! I cannot imagine such a thing occurring in a human-givens therapy session, as we are trained to keep focused on all aspects of what is occurring, so that we can stand back from the content and assess how best to work with the individual to address their difficulties and meet their goals. It is like keeping several balls in the air and is certainly not conducive to sleep. Our code of ethics also requires that we work only when we have spare capacity—being preoccupied with personal issues is a no-no.

But, as said, no therapist is perfect. It is also helpful that human givens therapists are encouraged to invite clients to complete outcome measures that track changes in symptoms and life satisfaction—and how well they felt heard by their therapist and able to raise what they wanted to talk about.

This isn’t a tick-box exercise, so that the therapist can bask in warm feelings and a sense of appreciation, although of course it is pleasing if one hits the mark. The questionnaires are usually completed online after the session, when the client, at one remove, is much more likely to feel able to admit the truth.

I am grateful for this. I had a client referred to me recently through the charity which offers free therapy to veterans and their families. (PTSD Resolution will only assign a human-givens practitioner to deliver this therapy.) In our first session, we built good rapport, I thought. However, in his feedback, the client mentioned that he had felt unable to ask whether I had a military background myself and shared that he felt distrustful of people outside the military family—he had been let down by civilians on many occasions.

At the next session, where I could see he was now a little uncomfortable about my having read what he had written, I first thanked him for being so honest and raising this issue. I told him that I did not have a military background and that, if he would feel more comfortable with a therapist who did, or had a military family, I could arrange this through the charity. He decided, because the issue had been aired, he was fine to continue; but I now recognised that I needed to pay special attention to enabling trust and be highly vigilant about explaining the purpose of the ideas I introduced.

We are all human, but there is no room for ego to get in the way when therapists are privileged to be entrusted with others’ deeply personal information and suffering.

item.title: Why Your Adult Child's Diagnosis May Be the Problem
item.description:
Parenting

Why Your Adult Child's Diagnosis May Be the Problem

Certainty about what's "wrong" with your adult child can block their growth.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • A diagnosis can offer parents relief but can also freeze an adult child to being seen as a fixed condition.
  • Curiosity is often what actually opens the door to repair.
  • Letting go of "knowing what's wrong" doesn't mean giving up; it can mean making room for your child to grow.

Parents of struggling adult children often reach out to ask the same question: "What's wrong with them?" I understand these parents are drained and fatigued and finally want a name for their adult child's often longstanding struggles. That's why I hear, "So, Dr. Jeff, could their problems come from their anxiety, depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder [ADHD], personality disorder, or maybe, you know, like something on the autistic spectrum?"

I understand why there is a hunt for a diagnosis or an unrelenting quest for one. A diagnosis promises structure. It says: This is a known thing, it has a shape, maybe even a treatment plan. After years of confusion and conflict, for parents of struggling adult children, "diagnostic certainty" can feel like solid ground. But what I've seen after decades of this work is that that cherished diagnosis, once it arrives, doesn't fully organize a parent's understanding. In fact, it can very often become the very problem it was supposed to solve.

If You Have a Hammer, Everything Can Look Like a Nail

What I have often seen play out is that when a parent decides they know what's "wrong" with their son or daughter, every future interaction gets filtered through that label. The eye-roll isn't just an eye-roll anymore. Instead, "that's their disorder talking." The missed phone call or text message isn't just a missed call or message. It's got to be their "ADHD/avoidance," which translates, unfortunately, to a symptom needing to be managed rather than a moment to be curious about. So, the search for a precise diagnostic label meant to bring clarity instead flattens a complicated adult human being into a diagnosis with legs.

Adult children tell me they feel this acutely. They sense when a parent has stopped seeing them and started seeing a diagnosis. That shift, from person to pathology, is often exactly what deepens the very estrangement or conflict the parent is trying to heal. The diagnosis becomes a lens that shows only what it's designed to, and the child living inside that lens starts to feel like there's no version of themselves their parent can see anymore. Rather, they feel seen only for the condition, or, even more colloquially (as a less flattering label), the family screw-up.

Curiosity Bridges Gaps and Creates Understanding

In my new book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!, I write about parents of adult children who've been blamed, sometimes fairly and sometimes not, for how their kids' lives have turned out. One pattern keeps showing up: Parents who move from assumption to curiosity give their child room to become someone beyond the label. Let me say this one more time for emphasis: I'm not against diagnoses. Some genuinely guide good treatment and can be a relief to a struggling adult child. But please keep in mind that a diagnosis is a starting hypothesis, not a life sentence.

The Takeaway

If you're a parent circling the question "What's wrong with them?" consider a harder but more freeing question: "What don't I understand yet?" That question is where the real work, along with a more connected relationship, actually begins.

item.title: Transforming Trauma Into Grace
item.description:
Post-Traumatic Growth

Transforming Trauma Into Grace

From the crush to the cornerstone.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Great trauma can lead to a deep, painful sense of powerlessness.
  • Traumatized individuals can gain resilience through the work of healing.
  • Posttraumatic growth can serve as the basis for great achievement.
Source: Konrad Gorecki / Shutterstock

There is a widely told story about a visitor who goes to the circus and asks the elephant trainer why the animal can be controlled by just a stake in the ground and a light chain. The trainer answers that the elephant doesn’t recognize its own strength because it’s been chained all its life. The animal doesn’t know it has the power to pull itself free and do what it wants.

The story is one most of us have heard, but many are unfamiliar with the practice that makes so many domesticated elephants ignorant of their power—a practice called phajaan. The Thai word means “the crush”—and it’s a cruel practice used to ensure young elephants taken from the wild never rebel against their trainers.

In phajaan, a young elephant is captured. In the months that follow, the young elephant is confined to a cage, its legs are restrained, and it’s beaten, stabbed, starved, and tormented with a bull hook. At the end of this barbaric process, the elephant is considered “broken,” and its handler believes it will never rebel.

The truth of the matter is that most of the elephants that undergo this experience are not broken. What they lack is trust—in themselves and in others. What these emotional animals carry is fear, anger, or grief (Samui Elephant Haven, 2025).

People who have experienced great trauma can adopt a similarly deep, painful sense of powerlessness. But, like the great elephant, we have strength within us that is waiting to be rediscovered and set free. It is within our power to pull up the stake, turn away from our tormentors, and know we can take care of ourselves.

The process by which this happens is growth—and it is the steady work of the subconscious that can help us transform our traumas to grace, as demonstrated by the following case example.

Posttraumatic Stress Disorder in an Adolescent

James, a 15-year-old athlete, was referred to work with me to deal better with anxiety stemming from his deeply troubled relationship with his father. Following his parents' divorce when he was 2, James divided his time between households until a heated argument led his father to suggest that James should leave. James did just that and moved permanently to his mother's home.

A subsequent reconciliation attempt with a therapist ended disastrously when the father told James he wished he had never been born, then argued with the therapist before storming out.

The aftermath left James with persistent nightmares, fear of his father appearing unexpectedly at his mother's house, and deep concern that he might inherit his father's propensity for anger and social alienation. These fears were grounded in real experience: His father had previously arrived at his mother's house, banged on the door, and called the police alleging kidnapping over a scheduling misunderstanding.

When I introduced James to his subconscious, he received calm guidance about becoming a better student and athlete, which was a gentle entry point into deeper work.

Later, we addressed his father's behavior, exploring the possibility that the father's destructive parenting represented the best he was capable of rather than deliberate cruelty. Notably, James's subconscious consistently pushed the therapy forward while James himself remained more cautious.

Over the following months, James built sufficient emotional resilience to attempt reconnecting with his father. Just before their first reconciliation meeting, his subconscious brought up a positive memory—a hike shared with his father four years earlier—reminding James that positive experiences between them had been possible.

I then asked a key question: If all the hardship with his father could be erased at the cost of losing the wisdom James had gained from dealing with his troubles, would James accept the trade? He said he would not. Thus, he recognized the important formative impact of his difficult experiences.

James and I started meeting with his father at a planned five-minute encounter and gradually lengthened the monthly meetings to 45-minute outings involving walks, sharing meals, and increasingly substantive conversations about the father's anger and how their relationship might improve.

When James eventually said that he was ready to meet his father independently, his father ceased all contact. James investigated enough to confirm his father was physically well, then accepted the situation with equanimity, understanding he bore no responsibility for his father's choices.

After two years of therapy, James had transformed remarkably. He became a high school newspaper writer and wrote some of his articles about trauma and resilience, and a sports team captain known for encouraging his teammates. In college, James founded a men's emotional support group, thus channeling his own hard-won healing into service for others.

From Self-Rejection to Grace

Traumatized individuals may not recognize their own self-worth and may reject themselves or be rejected by others (van der Kolk, 2014). Fortunately, as demonstrated by James’s recovery, the work of healing can lead to increased resilience and transformed self-understanding, which can become the cornerstone for great achievement (Tedeschi & Calhoun, 1996).

This is reminiscent of a passage from the Bible:

The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. (Ps. 118:22).

Jesus himself applied this passage to his own ministry, teaching that he was the cornerstone rejected by the builders (Matthew 21:42, Acts 4:11). History has repeatedly echoed this pattern:

Galileo Galilei was forced by the Inquisition in 1633 to recant his support for the idea that the sun was at the center of the solar system instead of a stationary Earth. Legend has it that he muttered in reference to the Earth, "and yet it moves." Of course, he was right (Finocchiaro, 1989).

Johann Sebastian Bach’s music was largely neglected after his death in 1750. Felix Mendelssohn revived Bach’s St. Matthew Passion in 1829. Thereafter, Bach’s music was rediscovered. He is now considered a pivotal figure in the history of Western music (Wolff, 2000).

Ignaz Semmelweis proposed in 1847 that doctors should wash their hands before delivering babies. He was ridiculed by the medical establishment, institutionalized, and died in an asylum. Within decades, the discovery that germs caused illness vindicated him completely (Keske, 2025).

Gregor Mendel presented the results of his genetics research in scientific forums regarding the fundamental laws of heredity in 1865. Yet, his studies were largely ignored for 35 years when they were rediscovered by three independent botanists who credited Mendel for his work (Vyskot & Siroky, 2022).

These cases are not merely historical curiosities but rather reflect a pattern that philosopher Thomas Kuhn identified as fundamental to how knowledge advances. He argued that truly revolutionary ideas are almost always rejected first, because they threaten how people understand the world, and their adoption would require much upheaval and rethinking. He termed this phenomenon paradigm shift (Kuhn, 1962).

Analogously, a patient may at first be unable or unwilling to conceive of any potential benefit from working through their trauma, but therapy can help shift their thinking, as an essential part of the healing process.

Takeaway

Viewing the work of recovery from trauma as possibly leading to worthy life achievement can act as a guiding light during dark times.

item.title: Still "Smearing the Queer"? Why the Use of LGBTQ Slurs Persists
item.description:
Sexual Orientation

Still "Smearing the Queer"? Why the Use of LGBTQ Slurs Persists

4 paths to reducing the use of harmful LGBTQ slurs.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • People use anti-LGBTQ slurs to harm/discipline others or reassure themselves about their own gender/sexuality.
  • Slurs are a microcosm of a larger societal system that is designed to maintain hetero-cis-normativity.
  • Slurs cause significant social harms.
  • Reducing LGBTQ slur use is possible online, in schools, and in communities.

We’ve all heard them. Queer. F*g. D*ke. These LGBTQ slurs are disturbingly common in everyday vernacular. They are fixtures in society.

But what motivates people to use LGBTQ slurs? Why are we still “smearing the queer”? What harms do LGBTQ slurs cause? What are some possible solutions?

Source: Rosemary Ketchum/Pexels

What Motivates People to Use LGBTQ Slurs?

LGBTQ slurs are everywhere—from day-to-day conversations, to social media, to shows, movies, and songs, we all hear LGBTQ slurs. But why? We likely don’t even realize what motivates someone to use LGBTQ slurs.

In my recent book, Interrogating the Use of LGBTQ Slurs: Still Smearing the Queer? (Worthen, 2024), I worked to uncover the mechanisms behind LGBTQ slur usage. I found that slurs are a very real microcosm of a larger societal system that is designed to maintain hetero-cis-normativity (the normative expectations that people should be both heterosexual and cisgender) (Worthen, 2020).

When someone uses an LGBTQ slur, they are participating in the active verbal admonishment of people they perceive as not meeting their expectations about gender and sexuality norms. They use these slurs to harm, to discipline, and to reassure themselves about their own gender/sexuality.

When that happens, the LGBTQ slur operates as a release valve in a situation where someone perceives a personal threat. I call this the queer adjustment. In efforts to assert and affirm one’s social power and secure hetero-cis-normativity, one uses an LGBTQ slur to stigmatize and discipline those perceived as not hetero-cis-normative enough. This helps to maintain a hierarchy that secures the privileged positions of those most invested in upholding hetero-cis-normativity and the devalued placement of LGBTQ people beneath them. LGBTQ slur use is a response bigots use to participate in The Queer Adjustment and police hetero-cis-normativity violations (Worthen, 2024).

Source: Pavel Danilyuk/Pexels

Are We Really Still “Smearing the Queer”?

Unequivocally yes. The ubiquity of LGBTQ slur use is palpable—for example, in the 2021 National School Climate Survey, nearly all LGBTQ students reported hearing homophobic remarks (Kosciw et al., 2022).

But not everyone feels the need to engage in the queer adjustment. Across a range of LGBTQ slurs, young men report substantially more LGBTQ slur usage when compared to older men and all women. In fact, the majority of slur-using culprits are young men, particularly a subset I refer to as “dude bros”—a brand of young men who display toxic masculinity through admonishment of anyone they perceive as weak (Worthen, 2021).

Studies investigating various forms of social media (e.g., Twitter/X) consistently demonstrate vast evidence of a wide range of LGBTQ slurs, most of which come from young men’s posts putting down others (Pascoe & Diefendorf, 2019; Ruberg, 2019). By all accounts, the schoolyard memories and/or historical narratives of games like “smear the queer” and other similar stories remain damaging fixtures in today’s society.

What Harms Do LGBTQ Slurs Cause?

When someone hears LGBTQ slurs, they can experience feelings of humiliation, dehumanization, oppression, disempowerment, and silencing (Popa-Wyatt & Wyatt, 2018). Some may even have responses similar to symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) inclusive of panic, mental duress, fear, anxiety, and vivid flashbacks of slur-involved incidents which can all have long term effects on an individual’s overall well-being, including increased suicidality (Jay, 2009). In fact, hearing LGBTQ slurs has been found to be related to numerous negative effects including higher levels of perceived danger and increases in hazardous alcohol and illicit drug use, headaches, poor appetite, and disturbed eating (Herek et al., 2002; Winberg et al., 2019; Woodford et al., 2012).

Source: Monstera Production/Pexels

But beyond the individual level, the regular use of LGBTQ slurs and their noticeable cultural presence work together to reinforce the continued oppression of LGBTQ people. Larger social harms such as decreased feelings of safety among LGBTQ people and vicarious victimization can happen when slur speech-motivated victimization incidents are widely publicized (Benier, 2017). By calling attention to the harms that LGBTQ slurs can cause, we can better understand how to work toward making the world a safer place for LGBTQ people.

4 Possible Areas to Reduce the Use of LGBTQ Slurs

Slurs hurt. Slurs harm. And slurs are powerful. But reducing LGBTQ slur use is possible, and we can do it by taking action in these 4 domains:

  1. In Schools: Implement anti-slur and anti-bullying policies; hire LGBTQ-supportive school staff; provide library books with age-appropriate LGBTQ content; acknowledge LGBTQ awareness days; establish LGBTQ-focused educational workshops, assignments, school-based special events, social clubs; display LGBTQ welcoming signage.
  2. In Communities: Elect LGBTQ-supportive leaders; provide LGBTQ educational classes and workshops; host LGBTQ community events; provide best practices training for first responders, healthcare workers, government-based providers, community service providers, and youth service leaders; establish community LGBTQ social groups; recognize LGBTQ awareness days; provide LGBTQ books at public libraries; display LGBTQ public art, museum exhibits, and welcoming signage (e.g., the rainbow flag).
  3. On Social Media: Implement anti-LGBTQ slur and anti-electronic harassment/cyberbullying policies; develop custom tools to express gender and sexual identities; offer safety measures and reporting features.
  4. Everywhere: Provide educational campaigns about the harms of LGBTQ slurs, deadnaming, and misgendering; enhance awareness about electronic harassment/cyberbullying; promote diversity, intersectionality, and LGBTQ issues; acknowledge LGBTQ political and historical figures and events; promote LGBTQ awareness days.

In a time when LGBTQ people are under attack, change is necessary. We can work together to reduce the cultural presence of LGBTQ slurs online, in schools, and in communities to make the world a safer place for LGBTQ people.

If you are experiencing distress, mental health concerns, or suicidal thoughts, get help 24/7 from a crisis counselor at The Trevor Project.

item.title: Teaching the Next Generation to Reject Misogyny
item.description:
Bias

Teaching the Next Generation to Reject Misogyny

Help children build equality, empathy, and healthier relationships with women.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Children learn how to value women by watching how adults speak about and treat other women.
  • Comparison fuels competition, but collaboration creates stronger families, communities, and futures.
  • Another woman's success is not your loss—there is room for every person to thrive.

Misogyny is often imagined as obvious hostility toward women: harassment, violence, discrimination, or openly declaring that women are less capable than men. But misogyny does not always announce itself so clearly.

Sometimes it appears in the belief that a confident woman is arrogant, while a confident man is a leader. It appears when mothers are expected to manage nearly every detail of family life yet are criticized regardless of their choices. It appears when women’s accomplishments are explained away, their appearance becomes available for public judgement, or their mistakes are judged more harshly than those of men.

Misogyny can also become internalized. Women may absorb negative cultural beliefs about their own gender and unknowingly repeat them.

Statements such as “Women are too dramatic,” “I prefer working with men,” or “She probably only succeeded because of her appearance” may seem like personal observations. However, they can reflect something women have been taught for generations: Other women are competitors, and only a limited number can succeed.

Misogyny Has Been Written Into the Law

These messages did not develop in a vacuum. Throughout American history, women were legally treated as less independent, less capable, and less entitled to power than men.

For most of the nation’s history, women could not vote. The 19th Amendment, ratified in 1920 after decades of activism, prohibited denying voting rights based on sex. Even then, discriminatory state laws and practices continued to prevent many women of color from voting.

In the United States, under the legal tradition of coverture, a married woman’s identity was historically absorbed into her husband’s. Depending on the time and state, married women faced restrictions on owning property, controlling earnings, entering contracts, and initiating legal proceedings independently.

Women could also be denied jobs simply because they were women or dismissed because they became pregnant. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibited employment discrimination based on sex. The Pregnancy Discrimination Act of 1978 later clarified that discrimination involving pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions constitutes unlawful sex discrimination.

Financial independence was restricted as well. Before federal protections were enacted in the 1970s, lenders could require women to obtain male co-signers or treat applicants differently because of sex or marital status. Today, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act prohibits discrimination in credit transactions based on characteristics including sex and marital status.

article continues after advertisement

Educational opportunities were similarly unequal. Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 prohibited sex-based discrimination in federally funded educational programs and activities, helping expand women’s access to academics, athletics, scholarships, and professional preparation.

These legal changes represent extraordinary progress. Yet their recency matters. Women living today remember being denied credit, excluded from professional opportunities, or expected to leave their jobs when they became pregnant.

When opportunities have historically been scarce, competition can begin to feel like survival.

Source: George Milton / Pexels

The Myth That Only One Woman Can Win

Even after laws change, cultural beliefs can remain.

Women may still receive the message that there is room for only one successful female executive, physician, author, athlete, entrepreneur, or community leader. When another woman succeeds, her accomplishment may feel less like inspiration and more like evidence that an opportunity has disappeared.

But success is not a pie with a limited number of slices.

Another woman’s promotion does not reduce your opportunity. Her thriving business does not invalidate your ideas. Her child’s accomplishment is not proof that you are failing as a parent. Her appearance, relationship, home, or career is not a verdict on your worth.

Comparison becomes particularly damaging when we compare our private struggles with another person’s public presentation. Social media allows us to view carefully selected moments while hiding the conflict, rejection, exhaustion, uncertainty, and sacrifice behind them.

A healthier response is not, “She is better than me.” It is, “Her life is different from mine.” And more importantly, “This is a reflection of her highlight reel, not her real life”.

article continues after advertisement

What Parents Can Do

Children learn beliefs about women long before they can define misogyny.

They notice whether daughters are expected to help more around the house. They notice whether boys are praised for being assertive while girls are labeled bossy. They hear adults criticize women’s bodies, parenting choices, voices, clothing, ambition, and aging.

Parents can interrupt these messages.

Teach girls that their worth does not depend on beauty, popularity, agreeableness, or perfection. Praise their curiosity, courage, creativity, integrity, and effort. Let them disagree respectfully, take up space, make mistakes, and develop ambitions without apologizing for them.

Teach boys that girls are equals, not prizes, caretakers, or supporting characters. Expect boys to participate in household labor, express emotions responsibly, respect boundaries, and see empathy as strength.

Most importantly, let children witness women supporting women.

Avoid gossip that tears other women down. Speak positively about female leaders, colleagues, relatives, and friends. Recommend women for opportunities. Share their work. Celebrate their victories without immediately comparing them to your own life.

When jealousy appears, become curious rather than ashamed. Another woman’s success may reveal something you want, but it does not require you to resent her for having it.

There is enough creativity, leadership, purpose, and meaningful success for every woman in the world—although success will not look the same for everyone.

Our daughters are watching how women speak about themselves and one another. Our sons are learning how women deserve to be treated.

When adults replace comparison with confidence and competition with collaboration, children learn that another person’s success is not a threat.

It is proof of what may be possible.

item.title: Still Hoping for the Fountain of Youth?
item.description:
Creativity

Still Hoping for the Fountain of Youth?

To maintain youthfulness, try on the fine arts.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • It's never too late to learn to play a musical instrument, or draw, or even listen to music.
  • According to experts, we need to trust that we are creative and look for ways to foster that creativity.
  • A trip to a local museum, an art exhibit, or even listening to music, can meet the the research criteria.
Mythical Fountain of Youth
Source: Margaret Giatrasan / Unsplash

Although we know it’s a myth, as we age, many of us continue to search for the proverbial fountain of youth so that we can turn back the clock, or age more slowly. What is it about aging that worries us so much? Is it the bodily changes, the loss of purpose, the mind getting dull—or something still worse?

While several of our current tech leaders try stringent or bizarre diets, unproven drugs, and novel body strengthening routines that are beyond the reach of most of us, there may be simpler, enjoyable, and less costly alternatives to maintaining our youthfulness that are satisfying—and that work.

A research team at the University of London “found that those who engaged in arts and cultural activities more frequently, and who engaged in a wider diversity of these activities, appeared to have a slower pace of ageing and a younger biological age….” The study went on to say that “The links were stronger for middle-aged and older adults aged 40 or above,” meaning that it’s never too late to invest yourself in activities like learning to play a musical instrument, or drawing, or even listening to music—yes, just listening!

More striking still was the observation that those who engaged in the arts, at least once a week, aged more slowly than those who did physical exercise once a week. So there is even hope for the self-proclaimed couch potato. When I suggest findings like this to my age cohort—older adults—I usually hear that such endeavors require creativity. And then there is the usual follow-up argument that details how they are just not creative, never have been, as if there is an on-off switch on this commodity. Lots of folks believe that you either have creativity or you don’t. Is that dichotomy valid?

Is Creativity Inherent or Learned?

Everyone is born with the ability to be creative, as witnessed in toddlers’ art classes. It is true that some kids are early identified as gifted and then get lots of support for their art form. Most others don’t pursue drawing or playing the violin because they don’t see themselves as creative and aren’t encouraged by parents or the community at large. I know this to be true. You don’t have to feel creative to enjoy the arts.

When I was writing my book, The Vintage Years: Finding Your Inner Artist (Writer, Musician, Visual Artist) After Sixty, I interviewed many people, some of whom abandoned a creative pursuit as a child or teen because it became too difficult to motivate themselves when they received no support or encouragement from the outside world. They believed they didn’t have creativity.

I also interviewed some, like David Finkel, now retired cellist with the world-renowned Emerson String Quartet and current co-artistic director of the Chamber Music Society at Lincoln Center in New York City. He was, in fact, encouraged in his cello playing as a child by his family who were also musicians, and he was early identified as gifted—offering the necessary boost to his self-belief. He was labeled as creative and internalized the moniker. But he is certainly in the minority.

Recently I heard Aithan Shapira, an artist who is also a lecturer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, talk about “creative maturation,” a process that needs tending like a garden. He is a believer in the creativity of us all, but he says that the garden does need to be tended to—and pruned as necessary. He calls this “destruction in the service of growth.” In a talk at the Modern Elder Academy,* he questioned whether “we are enabling the things that emerge.” We need to trust that we are creative and look for ways to foster our own creativity to breathe life into it. Creativity, after all, is not an on/off switch or only available to some, and not others.

Virginia Kidd, Ph.D.,** a retired professor of communication studies, spoke with me about this conundrum. She suggested that while we all have novel ideas, they’re often dismissed as unimportant by ourselves. She said, “I get ideas, and while other people get ideas as well, they often ignore them and say ‘No. I can’t do that.’ When people say no, they don’t have space to pursue new ideas.” They are shutting off a channel to creative processes.

It’s hard to support a creative inclination when there are naysayers all around you, and also within you. In our early years, taken up mostly in school, there are lots of distractions and challenges that need to be met—no time for creative activities to be taken seriously, according to the doubters. In midlife, people are just too busy with family, work, and community to be distracted by a creative pursuit.

Embracing Creativity Later in Life

But later in life, when things slow down a bit, the yearning to play the piano, or write that short story that’s been developing in your head, or take that pottery class at the senior center becomes easier to integrate into life, and more like an urgency as time feels like it’s running out. Still, the nagging worry about how you aren’t creative may once again come to the fore. Now is the time to challenge this, for if not now, then when? What's more, a trip to a local museum, art exhibit, or even listening to music can meet the University of London criteria.

The creativity paradigm really needs to be changed. Just assume that you are as creative as you need to be. Then the pursuit becomes easier. You are engaging in whatever activity you like because you want to, independent of creativity. It makes life easier, and there are fewer barriers to overcome. The bonus is that you will probably live longer and enjoy your life a bit more.

*Modern Elder Academy (MEA), Live Event, June 25, 2026, “The Art of Change: Creativity as Fuel for Growth in Uncertain Times"

**California State University, Sacramento

item.title: AI and the iPod Test
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI and the iPod Test

Why are so many people reaching for "obsolete" tech?

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • The iPod may represent a test of whether your own mind still comes first.
  • This relates to AI taking small daily acts of thinking off your hands.
  • Nobody defends this loss the way labor once fought automation. It just goes unnoticed.
Source: Image by Mike Foster from Pixabay.

Maybe you shouldn't throw away that old iPod.

A recent Harvard Gazette article on the "tech-lash" caught my attention. It was built around an interview with the analyst Sara Watson where she talked about people digging up vintage iPods and going back to flip phones, part of a broader turn toward what she called "grandma hobbies" like knitting.

Watson also used an emerging term, "friction-maxxing," where steps are deliberately reintroduced into a task to counteract technology designed to be frictionless. Further, she pointed to resistance to surveillance capitalism, to the inevitability framing tech companies keep selling us and to the sense that our devices were changed without our consent. She also ties it to the body and the tactile pleasure of a mechanical engagement.

All good points, and I don't think she's wrong. Watson's perspective explains why people are irritated. But it doesn't explain what they are trying to preserve. And that might be even more important.

What the iPod Doesn't Do

An iPod doesn't choose the next song based on what keeps you listening longest. It doesn't know you. It has no opinion about your taste and basically nothing to optimize. You loaded it once, and after that it just played what you told it to play.

That's not nostalgia. It's a description of a device with no theory of you.

Compare that to a device that finishes your sentences and suggests what comes next, from routes to tunes. Each of those is a convenience and none of them, on their own, costs you anything you'd notice. Now here's the critical difference. Convenience arrives in increments too small to argue with, and at some point the increments add up to a changed relationship with your own mind.

Watson calls this a market response, a form of consumer resistance. Maybe. But I keep thinking about something more specific than resistance: the difference between a mind that is still practicing and one that has stopped without announcing it.

Activities of Daily Thinking

A few months ago I proposed a conceptual framework called Activities of Daily Thinking (ADTs) that was borrowed directly from the clinical language of Activities of Daily Living (ADLs). These are the basic tasks like dressing or preparing food that clinicians use as a proxy for independence. My suggestion was that thinking has its own version of that checklist that included reading, writing, deciding, disagreement, and contemplation. Small, everyday acts. No single one is missed the day it stops and that's exactly the problem.

article continues after advertisement

The iPod trend looks to me like ADT showing up as behavior, not just market adoption.

Taken individually, each act on that list seems almost trivial. Choosing your own playlist doesn't really make you a sharper thinker. But no single act was ever the point. The real question is what happens to a mind that keeps outsourcing them.

I use AI every day and I'm not making an argument against artificial intelligence. It's an argument for recognizing that effort sometimes has value independent of efficiency.

Thinking for Yourself

Here's where I think the Gazette piece stops short. Watson's four levers—law, norms, market, architecture, borrowed from Lawrence Lessig—are all external. They describe forces acting on a person. None of them describe what happens inside the person who keeps handing off the small daily acts of thinking and deciding.

The Luddites weren't fighting looms, they were fighting the loss of work and the social structure, and Watson is right to make that distinction. But there's no equivalent labor movement forming around the loss of your own mind on your own problems. Simply put, there's no picket line for a habit no one notices you losing.

I don't know if the iPod people would put it this way. Maybe it really is mostly about ad-free listening and owning your files outright. But I'd bet at least some of them, if pressed, would land somewhere close to wanting one part of the day where nothing was trying to think for them.

item.title: Psychoanalytic Object Relations Through Song
item.description:
Psychoanalysis

Psychoanalytic Object Relations Through Song

A closer look at John Mayer's "Daughters" and psychoanalytic object relations.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Our earliest bonds echo through every relationship.
  • What we don't examine eventually shapes us.
  • Parents provide a child's first blueprint for love and security.
Source: Ground Picture / Shutterstock

When teaching psychoanalytic principles as a professor, I like bringing in relatable cultural examples to highlight theory.

One of them is the 2003 John Mayer song, "Daughters" (released on his breakthrough album Heavier Things). Though the song is more than two decades old, it remains a timeless blueprint for understanding the mechanics of psychoanalytic object relations.

Whether Mayer himself ever reclined on the analyst’s couch to listen to the ticking metronome of his own unconscious, or perhaps it was simply his formidable intellect, talent, and sensitivity to human emotions that allowed him to forge this understanding, "Daughters" stands as a superlative example of how early attachments set the stage for future love relationships.

Object Relations and Early Imprinting

Psychoanalytic object relations shifts from traditional Freudian theory of purely drive-based or intrapsychic conflicts toward the fundamental human need for connection and attachment with primary caregivers. This relational landscape was mapped by object psychoanalysts such as D.W. Winnicott, Melanie Klein, W.R.D. Fairbairn, Margaret Mahler, John Bowlby, and Jessica Benjamin, whose collective work illuminates the nuances of early bonding, parent dynamics, and psychological development.

Several core concepts define the object relations theory:

  • The Internalized Imago: Children do not merely interact with their parents; they internalize them, creating mental representations and internal working models of self and other.
  • The Paternal and Maternal Bridges: Object relations recognizes both parents as vital external figures (objects) who help the growing child navigate separation, validation, and trust in the wider world.
  • Repetition Compulsion: When an early object—such as a mother or father—is emotionally absent, inconsistent, rejecting, or abusive, the developing child falls into a subconscious pattern of recreating those previous parental dynamics in present relationships, endlessly attempting to rewrite an unexamined past.
Source: Shutterstock

Lyrical Analysis

As we look at the lyrics of "Daughters," we see Mayer describe a relationship at a crossroads.

I know a girl

She puts the color inside of my world

But she's just like a maze

Where all of the walls all continually change

From an object relations standpoint, the shifting walls of the "maze" describe his partner caught in relational ambivalence. Because her foundational caregivers were unpredictable or emotionally unavailable, her internal world is structured around instability. Since she could not attain a secure attachment in early childhood, she struggles to form a stable bond with a prospective partner in the here and now.

Separating the Partner From the Imago

And I've done all I can

To stand on her steps with my heart in my hands

Now I'm starting to see

Maybe it's got nothing to do with me

This section captures a vital clinical realization. Mayer recognizes that his partner’s guardedness is not his personal failure, but a projection on her part. In object relational terms, she's not reacting to the person standing in front of her; she's reacting to her internal imago—the internalized representation of a caregiver who failed to show up. As such, her inability to fully receive love is an artifact of a traumatic developmental history.

The Intergenerational Blueprint

Fathers, be good to your daughters

Daughters will love like you do.

Girls become lovers who turn into mothers

So mothers be good to your daughters too

Here, the song directly aligns with the thesis of intergenerational trauma transmission within object relations theory. Parents provide a child's first blueprint for love and security. If that foundational template is damaged, the structure of all future adult attachments will be compromised. Mayer's song asserts a profound psychoanalytic truth: Unhealed early wounds do not simply disappear—they shift into relational sabotage, shaping how we love, partner, and ultimately pass down those patterns to our own children.

Closing Notes

In "Daughters," John Mayer operationalizes object relations theory for a mainstream audience. He urges parents to form meaningful, good attachments with their children, for romantic partners to learn when issues are projections and to understand the power of knowing your own narrative. "Daughters" transcends music and poetry, echoing Carl Jung’s famous maxim: "Until you make the unconscious conscious, it will direct your life and you will call it fate."

The focus of meaningful psychoanalytic treatment is to map direct lines from fractured early object relationships, unravel the defenses that prevent adult intimacy, and transform ruptures into conscious awareness so more adaptive ways of living—and loving—can occur.

item.title: Psychedelic Integration Is Reflected in How You Live
item.description:
Psychedelics

Psychedelic Integration Is Reflected in How You Live

Why lasting change after psychedelics is measured by how we love, communicate, and belong.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Psychedelic insight and psychological integration are not the same thing.
  • Because many of our deepest patterns develop in relationships, lasting change often unfolds there.
  • Integration becomes visible through gradual changes in how we communicate, repair, trust, and belong.
Source: Oussama Amrouche / Pexels

Psychedelics are everywhere these days—books, television, movies, and even government research. The growing interest in psychedelic therapy has brought renewed attention to the idea of integration, or how to make what was learned in the psychedelic journey something real, relevant, and usable in the person’s life. Examples include journaling, meditation, spending time in nature, creating art, attending integration circles, continuing psychotherapy, or working with an integration coach, of which I am one. These practices can all be deeply valuable because they create space to reflect on experiences that can be difficult to understand, let alone put into words.

As helpful as these recommendations are, they also invite a deeper one: Are people actually integrating what they experienced? Because when people talk about integration, sometimes they mean making sense of an experience. Sometimes integration describes the practices that follow a journey. Sometimes it simply means holding onto what was learned. Each of these captures an important part of the process, but none fully describes what psychological integration actually is and how we make use of it in our daily lives.

From Insight to Daily Life

From a psychological perspective, integration is the gradual process through which insight becomes incorporated into everyday life. It is the movement from understanding ourselves differently to living differently because of that understanding. Insight may arrive suddenly, but integration unfolds over time. It becomes visible as our relationships, our decisions, and our responses to everyday challenges begin to reflect something that once existed only as an idea or a fleeting experience.

This distinction is important because psychedelic experiences can offer moments of extraordinary clarity. Someone may recognize how often they sacrifice their own needs to maintain harmony. Another person may discover that beneath years of perfectionism lies an enduring fear of not being enough. Someone else may experience genuine compassion toward themselves after decades of self-criticism. These realizations can fundamentally reshape how we understand our lives, and they deserve to be taken seriously.

Turning Understanding Into Action

Understanding ourselves, however, is not the same as living differently. A person may recognize that they avoid conflict while continuing to apologize for needs they have every right to express. They may understand that vulnerability creates intimacy while still finding it nearly impossible to tell someone they are hurt. They may experience profound self-acceptance during a psychedelic journey yet continue to question, months later, whether they are worthy of receiving love from another person. Insight can emerge in a matter of hours. Living from that insight often requires months or years of integrated practice.

This is why I have come to think differently about where integration actually occurs. While individual practices remain important, many of the changes people hope for cannot develop in isolation. Our expectations about closeness, trust, conflict, belonging, and emotional safety were shaped through relationships long before we had language to describe them. We learned whether expressing emotion brought comfort or criticism, whether asking for help was welcomed or discouraged, whether mistakes threatened connection, and whether we could remain fully ourselves without risking rejection. These experiences became templates for how relationships work.

The Role of Relationships

Because these patterns developed in relationship, many of them are transformed in relationship as well. A journal may help us recognize that we fear disappointing other people. Meditation may help us notice the anxiety that accompanies vulnerability. Reflection may deepen our understanding of why certain situations feel emotionally charged. Eventually, however, another person becomes part of the process.

We discover what it feels like to express disappointment without destroying the relationship. We learn that disagreement does not inevitably lead to abandonment. We experience receiving care without immediately feeling indebted, or apologize without collapsing into shame, and set boundaries without believing we have become selfish or unlovable.

These moments rarely feel as dramatic as a psychedelic journey. They are also the moments that often reveal whether integration is taking place. They demonstrate that insight has moved beyond intellectual understanding and begun to reshape the way we relate to ourselves and to others.

Over the years, I have found myself asking different questions than many people expect after a psychedelic experience. Rather than focusing primarily on the intensity of the journey or the symbolism of what occurred, I become curious about everyday life. Is this person becoming more honest with the people they love? Are they asking for help more directly? Can they remain present during difficult conversations instead of withdrawing or becoming defensive? Do they recover from misunderstandings more quickly? Are they becoming more capable of receiving care without questioning whether they deserve it? These questions may sound like questions about relationships, but they are also questions about integration.

Although I am writing here about psychedelic experiences, I believe this understanding extends well beyond them. Meaningful psychotherapy, profound spiritual experiences, grief, serious illness, becoming a parent, or falling deeply in love can all change how we understand ourselves. Regardless of how insight arrives, it eventually encounters the same challenge. It must become something we practice until it is reflected not only in what we believe about ourselves but also in how we live with other people.

Perhaps this is why I have become less interested in measuring transformation by the intensity of an experience. Extraordinary moments can open doors that once seemed permanently closed, but they cannot walk us through those doors. Lasting change is revealed in the ordinary moments that follow: the difficult conversation that unfolds differently than it once would have; the boundary expressed with kindness rather than fear; the willingness to repair after conflict; the growing capacity to receive love without pushing it away; and the quiet realization that belonging no longer requires abandoning ourselves.

Ultimately, integration is not measured by how vividly we remember a psychedelic journey or how eloquently we describe it, although they may be important parts of the process. It is measured by whether our lives gradually begin to reflect what we discovered. When we find ourselves loving with greater openness, communicating with greater honesty, repairing relationships with greater humility, and belonging without sacrificing who we are, the experience has become more than a meaningful memory. It has become part of the architecture of a life.
